messages.content: "In a physics experiment, you are given two charges. The first charge has a magnitude of 5 coulombs and the second charge has a magnitude of 10 coulombs. These charges are placed at a distance of 2 meters from each other. You are asked to calculate the electromagnetic force between these charges. You perform the experiment twice. The first time, the charges are placed in a vacuum, which has a permittivity of 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m. The second time, the charges are placed in a medium with a relative permittivity of 5 x 10^-12 F/m. Can you calculate the electromagnetic force between the charges in both scenarios?"

function.name: electromagnetic_force
function.description: Calculate the electromagnetic force between two charges placed at a certain distance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

charge1.description: The magnitude of the first charge in coulombs.

charge2.description: The magnitude of the second charge in coulombs.

distance.description: The distance between the two charges in meters.

medium_permittivity.description: The relative permittivity of the medium in which the charges are present. Default is 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m (vacuum permittivity). This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Coulomb’s law**

\[
F \;=\; \frac{k\,q_1\,q_2}{r^{2}}, \qquad 
k \;=\; \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon}
\]

where  

* \(q_1 = 5\;\text{C}\)  
* \(q_2 = 10\;\text{C}\)  
* \(r = 2\;\text{m}\;\;\Rightarrow\; r^{2}=4\;\text{m}^{2}\)

---

## 1.  Vacuum

\[
\varepsilon_{\text{vac}} = \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}
\]

\[
k_{\text{vac}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
               = \frac{1}{4\pi(8.854\times10^{-12})}
               \approx 8.9876\times10^{9}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2
\]

\[
F_{\text{vac}} = \frac{8.9876\times10^{9}\;(5)(10)}{4}
               = 8.9876\times10^{9}\times12.5
               \approx 1.12\times10^{11}\;\text{N}
\]

---

## 2.  Medium with “permittivity” \(5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\)

> **Note:** The value given ( \(5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\) ) is an *absolute* permittivity, not a relative permittivity.  
> (If the intent were a relative permittivity of 5, the calculation below would be different.)

\[
\varepsilon_{\text{med}} = 5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}
\]

\[
k_{\text{med}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{\text{med}}}
               = \frac{1}{4\pi(5\times10^{-12})}
               \approx 1.5915\times10^{10}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2
\]

\[
F_{\text{med}} = \frac{1.5915\times10^{10}\;(5)(10)}{4}
               = 1.5915\times10^{10}\times12.5
               \approx 1.99\times10^{11}\;\text{N}
\]

---

### Summary

| Scenario | Permittivity \(\varepsilon\) | Coulomb constant \(k\) | Force \(F\) |
|----------|------------------------------|------------------------|-------------|
| Vacuum | \(8.854\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\) | \(8.99\times10^{9}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\) | \(\boxed{1.12\times10^{11}\;\text{N}}\) |
| Medium (given \(\varepsilon = 5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\)) | \(5\times10^{-12}\;\text{F/m}\) | \(1.59\times10^{10}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\) | \(\boxed{1.99\times10^{11}\;\text{N}}\) |

---

#### What if the medium had a *relative* permittivity of 5?

If the medium’s relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r = 5\) (dimensionless), then

\[
\varepsilon_{\text{med}} = \varepsilon_r\,\varepsilon_0 = 5(8.854\times10^{-12}) = 4.427\times10^{-11}\;\text{F/m}
\]

\[
k_{\text{med}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{\text{med}}} \approx 1.80\times10^{9}\;\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2
\]

\[
F_{\text{med}} \approx 2.25\times10^{10}\;\text{N}
\]

In this case the force would be **smaller** than in vacuum, as expected when the medium has a higher permittivity.
